newsitem.title: GERMANY: German union boss says 32-hr week would boost jobs.
newsitem.headline: German union boss says 32-hr week would boost jobs.

text.p: Germany should shorten its working week to 32 hours to open jobs for its more than four million unemployed and aid the drive to qualify for European monetary union (EMU), a union leader said on Tuesday.

Germany's ability to meet the criteria for EMU was directly connected to the country's "extreme, high unemployment", Klaus Zwickel, head of Germany's largest union IG Metall, told workers at car maker Volkswagen AG.

"I am convinced that the securing and creation of jobs is to be realised best by a general reduction of work times," Zwickel said, repeating his suggestion from last week for a four-day week in large companies.
Zwickel, who said the metalworking union supported the idea of a single European currency, also warned against putting too much emphasis on strict interpretations of EMU criteria.
He also blamed government austerity efforts for pushing jobless queues to near-record levels.
"The overemphasis on binding fiscal convergence criteria is wrong," he said, adding that Europe should strive for social and labour unity as well as economic and monetary union.
"For us it is important that the largest number of countries enter (EMU) as possible," he said.
Germany, which had 4.5 million unemployed in March, could put almost half that number back to work by reducing overtime and shortening the work week, he said.
Wages could be adjusted so that unions, government and employers could each absorb the cost for one hour less per week, he said.

"Work must be justly distributed for everyone and everyone must share in the increase of productivity," he told workers at VW, which introduced a short working week with the agreement of unions to protect jobs during a recent downturn in sales.
Reforms proposed by Bonn to lower labour overhead costs, taxes and pension contributions would increase the burden on workers and lead to "uncontrolled, pure capitalism", he said.

He also criticised corporations for failing to add staff even as profits were on the rise. "In spite of the improvement in economic conditions, they are using 'globalisation' to put the blame on the workers and unions," he said.
